lines.text: The Air Force is offering about four thousand seven hundred acres of Alaska for A I data centers.
Some sits at Eielson Air Force Base, outside Fairbanks, where bills are among the nation's highest.
Does that shrink a Fairbanks bill or grow it? One number decides. The offering doesn't say.
Nothing's awarded. Alaskans took positions anyway.
Salcha resident Sarah Hollister told reporters the jets always meant sacrifice.
Swap that for a data center's hum, she said, and we've lost our way.
Fairbanks asked for a pause, on both its state and federal lists.
Senator Lisa Murkowski says Alaska can't support them on an insecure energy base.
She didn't say the land. She said the power.
The Air Force calls it a partnership supporting its Airmen and Guardians.
Your bill is wires and fuel. The wires split across everyone, so that half is tall.
A giant customer helps pay for them either way. That half thins.
The fuel bites. A big load either brings its own power, or competes for what's here.
So it turns on how big. And how big is what nobody has published.
Mayor Grier Hopkins says defense spending buoyed Fairbanks when the F thirty fives came.
But a fighter wing comes with a budget. A data center comes with an appetite.
So the ask isn't megawatts. Nobody can publish those yet.
Ask for the date. Does that number go public before the land is leased?
The terms aren't written. That's the opening.
